measure.subtitle: Type it, tap it, or use the camera. Every entry is checked before it is saved.

history.title: History
history.subtitle: How your numbers changed over time.

emergency.title: Emergency procedure
emergency.subtitle: Work through the steps in order. Stop at the first step that solves the problem.
emergency.autonomous: Earth help is hours away — the crew leads care.

steps.self_care: Rest, follow the guidance on screen and measure again in a few minutes.
steps.crew_medical_officer: Tell the Crew Medical Officer what you feel and show your latest values.
steps.flight_surgeon: Call the flight surgeon on the medical channel and describe the situation.
steps.emergency: Start the emergency protocol: call the whole crew, secure the person and begin life support.

settings.title: Settings
settings.subtitle: Environment, language, units and demo data.

meaning.nominal: Within the normal range. Keep your routine.
meaning.advisory: Worth knowing. No action needed right now.
meaning.caution: Slightly outside normal. Follow the guidance and measure again.
meaning.warning: Clearly outside normal. Follow the steps and inform the person shown.

systolicBP.label: Systolic blood pressure
systolicBP.description: The top number of a blood-pressure reading: how hard your blood pushes on artery walls when your heart beats.
systolicBP.howTo: Sit still for 5 minutes, strap yourself in, wrap the cuff on your bare upper arm at heart level and start the monitor. Do not talk during the reading.

diastolicBP.label: Diastolic blood pressure
diastolicBP.description: The bottom number of a blood-pressure reading: the pressure in your arteries while your heart rests between beats.
diastolicBP.howTo: Recorded together with systolic pressure by the same cuff reading.

heartRate.label: Resting heart rate
heartRate.description: How many times your heart beats per minute while you are calm and still.
heartRate.howTo: Rest for 5 minutes. Use the pulse oximeter, the cuff reading, or count your wrist pulse for 30 seconds and double it.

bloodGlucose.label: Blood sugar (fasting)
bloodGlucose.description: How much sugar (glucose) is in your blood before breakfast. It is your body's main fuel.
bloodGlucose.howTo: Before eating, wash and dry a fingertip, prick the side of it with a lancet and touch the drop to the meter strip. Capture the lancet safely — it can float away.

bodyTemp.label: Body temperature
bodyTemp.description: How warm your body is inside. A rise can mean infection; in weightlessness it naturally runs a little higher.
bodyTemp.howTo: Use the in-ear or under-tongue thermometer after 15 minutes without eating, drinking or exercising.

sleepHours.label: Sleep
sleepHours.description: Hours you actually slept in the last 24 hours. Noise, light and stress in space often cut sleep short.
sleepHours.howTo: Right after waking, enter the hours you slept (or read them from your actigraphy watch).

mood.label: Mood
mood.description: How you feel overall today, from 1 (very bad) to 5 (very good). Being honest helps the crew support each other.
mood.howTo: Once a day, in the evening, pick the face that matches your day. There is no wrong answer.

spo2.label: Blood oxygen (SpO₂)
spo2.description: The percentage of your red blood cells carrying oxygen. Low values can come from cabin air problems or lung trouble.
spo2.howTo: Clip the pulse oximeter on a warm fingertip, keep your hand still at heart level and wait for a steady number (about 30 seconds).

respRate.label: Breathing rate
respRate.description: How many breaths you take per minute at rest. Fast breathing can be an early warning sign.
respRate.howTo: Rest, then count how many times your chest rises in 30 seconds and double it. A crewmate can count for you.

radiationDose.label: Radiation dose
radiationDose.description: Radiation your body absorbed today, read from your personal dosimeter. The app adds it up across your whole career.
radiationDose.howTo: In the evening, read your personal dosimeter and enter today's value in millisieverts (mSv).

exerciseMinutes.label: Exercise
exerciseMinutes.description: Minutes of exercise today. In low gravity, bones and muscles weaken quickly without daily training.
exerciseMinutes.howTo: Enter the total minutes of treadmill, bike and resistance training you did today.

radiation.label: Space radiation
radiation.description: Outside Earth's protective magnetic field, energetic particles pass through the body and can damage cells and DNA. This raises long-term cancer risk and can affect the eyes, heart and brain.
radiation.countermeasures: Wear your dosimeter, follow shelter alerts during solar storms, and keep exposure as low as reasonably achievable.

isolation.label: Isolation & confinement
isolation.description: Living for months in a small space with the same few people can cause poor sleep, low mood, tension and fatigue.
isolation.countermeasures: Keep a regular sleep schedule, check in with your crewmates, talk to your support team and log your mood honestly.

distance.label: Distance from Earth
distance.description: The farther from Earth, the longer messages take and the harder it is to get help or come home. On Mars the crew must handle medical problems mostly on its own.
distance.countermeasures: Know your on-board medical kit and protocols; the Crew Medical Officer leads care and reports to the ground.

gravity.label: Altered gravity
gravity.description: Without normal gravity, body fluids shift toward the head, bones lose minerals, muscles shrink and balance changes. Returning to gravity can make you dizzy when standing up.
gravity.countermeasures: Exercise every day, stay hydrated, and stand up slowly after landing.

environment.label: Hostile & closed environment
environment.description: The spacecraft is a sealed bubble: air quality, CO₂, temperature, noise and microbes all affect your health.
environment.countermeasures: Watch cabin air readings, keep hygiene up, and report headaches or breathlessness early.

brain.label: Brain & mind
brain.function: Controls thinking, mood, sleep and every other body system.
brain.spaceRisk: Isolation, poor sleep and radiation can affect mood, focus and memory.

eyes.label: Eyes
eyes.function: Turn light into images and send them to the brain.
eyes.spaceRisk: Fluid shifting toward the head can swell the back of the eye (SANS) and blur vision; radiation raises cataract risk.

heart.label: Heart & blood vessels
heart.function: Pumps blood carrying oxygen and nutrients to the whole body.
heart.spaceRisk: In weightlessness the heart works less and can weaken; back in gravity, blood pressure may drop when standing.

lungs.label: Lungs
lungs.function: Bring oxygen into the blood and remove carbon dioxide.
lungs.spaceRisk: Cabin air problems (high CO₂, dust) and infections affect breathing and oxygen levels.

blood.label: Blood & metabolism
blood.function: Carries oxygen and fuel (sugar) and keeps energy balanced.
blood.spaceRisk: Inactivity and stress can disturb blood sugar control; space can change red blood cell counts.

bones.label: Bones
bones.function: Hold you up, protect organs and store calcium.
bones.spaceRisk: Without gravity, bones can lose about 1% of their mass per month — exercise slows this.

muscles.label: Muscles
muscles.function: Move the body and keep posture.
muscles.spaceRisk: Leg and back muscles shrink quickly when they don't carry weight.

immune.label: Immune system
immune.spaceRisk: Stress, radiation and poor sleep weaken immunity; dormant viruses can wake up.

kidneys.label: Kidneys
kidneys.function: Filter blood, balance fluids and control blood pressure.
kidneys.spaceRisk: Calcium from bones and low fluid intake raise the risk of kidney stones.

whole_body.label: Whole body (radiation)
whole_body.function: Radiation affects every cell; the total dose over a career matters most.
whole_body.spaceRisk: Higher cumulative dose raises long-term cancer risk; solar storms can deliver large doses in hours.

iss.label: Space station (ISS)
iss.description: Low Earth orbit. Weightless, mission control always reachable, return to Earth within about a day.

spacecraft.label: Deep-space spacecraft
spacecraft.description: Transit to the Moon or Mars. Weightless, higher radiation, growing signal delay, no quick way home.

rover.label: Pressurised rover
rover.description: Short surface trips in a small cabin. Watch air quality closely; exercise is limited.

lunar_base.label: Lunar base
lunar_base.description: One-sixth gravity, ~1.3 s signal delay, 3–5 days to return to Earth.

mars_base.label: Mars base
mars_base.description: About one-third gravity, up to ~24 min signal delay. The crew must manage medical events on its own.

nominal.label: Nominal
nominal.description: Healthy crew with normal day-to-day variation.

space_adaptation.label: Space adaptation
space_adaptation.description: First 3 days: motion sickness, fluid shift and poor sleep.

solar_particle_event.label: Solar particle event
solar_particle_event.description: A solar storm causes a sudden radiation spike; the crew shelters.

isolation_stress.label: Isolation stress
isolation_stress.description: Long Mars transit: sleep and mood slowly decline.

fever_dehydration.label: Fever & dehydration
fever_dehydration.description: One crew member develops a fever with fast heart rate.

orthostatic_return.label: Return to gravity
orthostatic_return.description: After landing, blood pressure drops when standing and heart rate rises.

mixed_mission.label: Mixed mission
mixed_mission.description: Default demo: four crew members, four stories — one healthy, one with an early fever, one with slowly worsening sleep and mood, one drifting from personal baseline.

radiation.underHalf: Career radiation dose is below half of the limit.
radiation.halfToEighty: Career radiation dose is between 50% and 80% of the limit.
radiation.overEighty: Career radiation dose is above 80% of the limit.

sustained.shortSleep: Less than 6.5 hours of sleep for 3 days in a row.
sustained.severeSleepLoss: Less than 4 hours of sleep for 2 days in a row.
sustained.noExercise: Less than 60 minutes of exercise for 3 days in a row.

alerts.title: Alert center
alerts.empty: No active alerts. All crew members nominal.

explanation.systolicBP: Blood pressure outside the normal range can signal dehydration, a fluid shift, or cardiovascular strain — all common in spaceflight.
explanation.diastolicBP: Diastolic pressure outside the normal range can point to the same fluid-shift and cardiovascular changes as systolic pressure.
explanation.heartRate: A resting heart rate far from normal can mean dehydration, fever, stress, or a cardiovascular problem that needs attention.
explanation.bloodGlucose: Blood sugar outside the normal range can affect energy, judgement and wound healing — important for a crew member who has to stay sharp.
explanation.bodyTemp: A body temperature outside the normal range often means infection, dehydration or heat/cold stress — easy to miss in a closed environment.
explanation.sleepHours: Too little sleep for too long impairs judgement, mood and immune function, and makes every other risk harder to catch.
explanation.mood: A low or falling mood can be an early sign of the psychological strain of isolation and confinement — one of the five spaceflight hazards.
explanation.spo2: Low blood oxygen can mean a cabin air problem or a lung/heart issue — both need fast attention in a sealed environment.
explanation.respRate: A breathing rate outside the normal range can signal a cabin air problem, anxiety, or a developing illness.
explanation.radiationDose: Space radiation raises long-term cancer and tissue-damage risk; a sudden spike can also mean a solar particle event in progress.
explanation.exerciseMinutes: Skipping exercise in microgravity or partial gravity speeds up bone and muscle loss that is hard to reverse later.

radiation.spe: {{metric}}: today's dose is far above what this environment normally sees — a solar particle event may be in progress.

rest.title: Rest and recover sleep debt
rest.step1: Protect your next sleep window — avoid caffeine and screens before it.
rest.step2: If you can, add a short nap and move non-essential tasks to tomorrow.

hydration.title: Rehydrate and cool down
hydration.step1: Drink water or an electrolyte solution steadily, not all at once.
hydration.step2: Loosen or remove extra layers and rest somewhere cooler if you can.

exercise.title: Get back on the exercise schedule
exercise.step1: Do today's exercise session even if it's shorter than usual.
exercise.step2: Resistance and cardio sessions are what slow bone and muscle loss.

nutrition.title: Check your last meal and timing
nutrition.step1: Eat a small balanced snack if it has been a while since your last meal.
nutrition.step2: Log what and when you ate so the trend is easy to read later.

medicationConsult.title: Flag it for a medical check
medicationConsult.step1: Note any symptoms you're feeling — dizziness, chest discomfort, shortness of breath.
medicationConsult.step2: Avoid strenuous activity until this has been reviewed.

radiationShelter.title: Reduce extra radiation exposure
radiationShelter.step1: Avoid EVA or other high-exposure activity until this has been reviewed.
radiationShelter.step2: Log the reading so the crew medical officer can see the trend.

radiationShelterSpe.title: Take shelter now
radiationShelterSpe.step1: Move to the designated radiation shelter immediately.
radiationShelterSpe.step2: Stay there until the flight surgeon or mission control confirms the event has passed.

psychSupport.title: Reach out and talk it through
psychSupport.step1: Talk to a crewmate, or use the scheduled private family conference.
psychSupport.step2: The crew medical officer can connect you with psychological support.

remeasure.title: Measure again
remeasure.step1: Re-take this measurement now to rule out a one-off reading error.
remeasure.step2: If it's still outside the normal range, follow the steps above.

contactCmo.title: Inform the crew medical officer
contactCmo.step1: Tell the crew medical officer this result and what you've already done about it.
contactCmo.step2: They decide whether this needs to go further.

contactFlightSurgeon.title: Contact the flight surgeon
contactFlightSurgeon.step1: Contact the flight surgeon now with this result and your symptoms.
contactFlightSurgeon.step2: Follow their instructions; the crew medical officer stays with you in the meantime.
contactFlightSurgeon.stepAutonomous1: Ground support is too far away to respond in time — the crew medical officer manages this now, following the autonomous protocol.
contactFlightSurgeon.stepAutonomous2: Send a report to the flight surgeon for the record; given the communication delay, do not expect a real-time reply.
